title: Segments, rays and lines
description: Questions on segments, rays, lines, their equations, circles, right angles and lines in space.

questions.question: Which points $$P + t(Q - P)$$ make up the segment $$PQ$$?
questions.explanation: $$t = 0$$ gives $$P$$, $$t = 1$$ gives $$Q$$, and the numbers in between give the points between (:ref{#segment-formula}). $$t \ge 0$$ gives a ray, and every $$t$$ gives the whole line.

questions.question: What point is a quarter of the way from $$P = (2, 1)$$ to $$Q = (10, -3)$$?
questions.explanation: $$Q - P = (8, -4)$$, and $$P + \frac{1}{4}(8, -4) = (4, 0)$$ (:ref{#fraction-along}). $$(8, -2)$$ is three quarters of the way, and $$(6, -1)$$ is the midpoint.

questions.question: $$d(P, Q) = 10$$ and $$X = P + 0.3(Q - P)$$. What are $$d(P, X)$$ and $$d(X, Q)$$?
questions.explanation: The point for $$t$$ is $$t\,d(P, Q)$$ from $$P$$ and $$(1 - t)\,d(P, Q)$$ from $$Q$$ (:ref{#fraction-along}): $$3$$ and $$7$$, which add up to $$10$$.

questions.question: How are the segments $$PQ$$ and $$QP$$ related?
options: They are the same set of points; the point for $$t$$ on one is the point for $$1 - t$$ on the other
They point opposite ways, so they are different sets
questions.explanation: A segment is a set of points with no order (:ref{#segment-symmetric}). Arrows are the ones where order matters: $$\overrightarrow{PQ}$$ and $$\overrightarrow{QP}$$ have opposite steps.

questions.question: What is the step of the arrow $$\overrightarrow{PQ}$$ from $$P = (1, 2)$$ to $$Q = (3, 7)$$?
questions.explanation: The step is end minus start, $$Q - P = (2, 5)$$ (:ref{#arrow}). $$(-2, -5)$$ is the step of $$\overrightarrow{QP}$$.

questions.question: The arrow from $$M = (4, -1)$$ is equivalent to $$\overrightarrow{PQ}$$, where $$P = (1, 2)$$ and $$Q = (3, 7)$$. Where does it end?
questions.explanation: Equivalent arrows have the same step (:ref{#arrow-equivalent}), so the end is $$M + (Q - P) = (4, -1) + (2, 5) = (6, 4)$$.

questions.question: Which condition says that $$\overrightarrow{PQ}$$ and $$\overrightarrow{MN}$$ are equivalent?
questions.explanation: $$N - M = Q - P$$ rearranges to $$P + N = Q + M$$ (:ref{#arrow-equivalent}): the diagonals $$PN$$ and $$QM$$ share a midpoint. Equal lengths alone allow arrows pointing different ways, and $$P + Q = M + N$$ says the segments $$PQ$$ and $$MN$$ share a midpoint.

questions.question: Which points make up the ray from $$P$$ in direction $$A$$?
questions.explanation: The ray starts at $$P$$ (at $$t = 0$$) and goes on forever in the direction of $$A$$ (:ref{#ray-formula}).

questions.question: Which point has the same direction as $$A = (2, -1)$$?
questions.explanation: Same direction means a positive multiple (:ref{#same-direction}). $$(6, -3) = 3A$$. $$(-4, 2) = -2A$$ has the opposite direction, and the other two are not multiples of $$A$$.

questions.question: The ray from $$P$$ in direction $$A$$ and the ray from $$P$$ in direction $$-2A$$: what are they?
options: The same ray, traced twice as fast
questions.explanation: A positive multiple of the direction gives the same ray (:ref{#ray-multiple}), but $$-2$$ is negative. Two rays from $$P$$ are the same exactly when their directions are the same direction (:ref{#rays-equal}).

questions.question: Which point is $$10$$ units from $$M = (1, 1)$$ in the direction of $$A = (3, 4)$$?
questions.explanation: $$|A| = 5$$, so the unit point is $$(\frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5})$$, and $$M + 10(\frac{3}{5}, \frac{4}{5}) = (7, 9)$$ (:ref{#arrow-given}). $$(31, 41)$$ uses $$10A$$, which is $$50$$ units long.

questions.question: Why is the zoom $$Z_{r,Q}(P) = Q + r(P - Q)$$ with $$r > 0$$ on the ray from $$Q$$ through $$P$$?
options: Because $$r(P - Q)$$ is shorter than $$P - Q$$
It is $$Q + tA$$ with $$A = P - Q$$ and $$t = r \ge 0$$
It isn't: it is on the opposite ray
questions.explanation: The ray from $$Q$$ through $$P$$ is the points $$Q + t(P - Q)$$ with $$t \ge 0$$, and the zoom is the one with $$t = r$$ (:ref{#zoom-on-ray}). Zooms with $$r \ne 1$$ don't keep distances, and $$r$$ may be larger than $$1$$.

questions.question: The slide $$T_A$$ with $$A \ne O$$ moves every point...
options: the distance $$|A|$$ in the direction of $$A$$
the distance $$|A|$$ in a direction that depends on the point
questions.explanation: The arrow from $$P$$ to $$P + A$$ has step $$A$$, the same as $$\overrightarrow{OA}$$ (:ref{#slide-direction}). So every point makes the same step.

questions.question: Which values of $$t$$ give the line through $$P$$ with direction $$A$$?
questions.explanation: A line goes on both ways, so $$t$$ can be positive, negative or zero (:ref{#line-formula}). Whole numbers would give equally spaced dots along it.

questions.question: Which describes the line through $$P = (1, 3)$$ and $$Q = (4, 1)$$?
questions.explanation: Start at $$P$$ and use the step $$Q - P = (3, -2)$$ as direction (:ref{#two-point-line}). Using $$Q$$ itself as the direction gives a line through $$P$$ that misses $$Q$$.

questions.question: Which pair of directions gives parallel lines?
questions.explanation: Lines are parallel when one direction is a non-zero multiple of the other (:ref{#parallel-formula}): $$(-3, -6) = -3(1, 2)$$. The test $$a_1b_2 - a_2b_1 = 1 \cdot (-6) - 2 \cdot (-3) = 0$$ agrees (:ref{#parallel-determinant}).

questions.question: Lines with directions $$(3, 2)$$ and $$(-6, 4)$$: how many points do they share?
options: It depends on where they start
questions.explanation: $$3 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot (-6) = 24 \ne 0$$, so the directions are not parallel, and lines that aren't parallel meet in exactly one point (:ref{#line-intersection}), wherever they start.

questions.question: Two parallel lines share one point. What can you conclude?
questions.explanation: Parallel lines are either the same line or never meet (:ref{#line-intersection}). Sharing a point rules out the second.

questions.question: Two ships at $$P + tA$$ and $$Q + tB$$ at time $$t$$ have paths that cross. When do they collide?
options: Never, since ships on different lines can't meet
When one value of $$t$$ gives $$P + tA = Q + tB$$
questions.explanation: Crossing paths only say the ships pass the same point, maybe at different times. A collision needs them there at the same time, so the same $$t$$ for both (see [Lines](./lines.mdx#crossing-paths-and-collisions)).

questions.question: Where do all the multiples $$tA$$ of a point $$A \ne O$$ lie?
questions.explanation: They are the points $$O + tA$$ for every $$t$$, the line through $$O$$ with direction $$A$$ (:ref{#multiples-line}). Negative $$t$$ gives the half of the line beyond $$O$$.

questions.question: Which equation describes the line through $$(1, 2)$$ with direction $$(3, -1)$$?
questions.explanation: By :ref{#line-equation}, $$a_2x - a_1y = a_2p_1 - a_1p_2$$ gives $$-x - 3y = -1 - 6$$, which is $$x + 3y = 7$$. Check with $$t = 1$$: $$(4, 1)$$ gives $$4 + 3 = 7$$. The equation $$3x - y = 1$$ has the direction's numbers as coefficients, which describes a perpendicular line.

questions.question: What is a direction of the line $$2x + 5y = 7$$?
questions.explanation: The line $$ax + by = c$$ has direction $$(-b, a)$$ (:ref{#equation-line}). Moving by $$(-5, 2)$$ changes $$2x + 5y$$ by $$-10 + 10 = 0$$. $$(2, 5)$$ is perpendicular to the line.

questions.question: Where does $$2x - y = 4$$ cross the $$y$$-axis?
questions.explanation: On the $$y$$-axis $$x = 0$$, so $$-y = 4$$ and $$y = -4$$. $$(2, 0)$$ is where it crosses the $$x$$-axis.

questions.question: What did this chapter prove that the Linear equations chapter took from the picture?
options: That every line passes through the origin
That every line has a slope
That the solutions of $$ax + by = c$$, with $$a$$ and $$b$$ not both $$0$$, form a straight line
That two equations always have one solution
questions.explanation: The solutions are exactly the line through one solution with direction $$(-b, a)$$ (:ref{#equation-line}), and every line has such an equation (:ref{#line-equation}). Vertical lines have no slope.

questions.question: Which line is parallel to $$4x - 6y = 1$$?
questions.explanation: $$ax + by = c$$ and $$a'x + b'y = c'$$ are parallel when $$ab' - a'b = 0$$ (:ref{#parallel-equations}): $$4 \cdot (-3) - 2 \cdot (-6) = 0$$. $$3x + 2y = 0$$ is perpendicular to it instead.

questions.question: Which line has no slope?
questions.explanation: $$x = 3$$ is vertical, with direction $$(0, 1)$$. Its first coordinate never changes, so there is no number of steps up per step across.

questions.question: How many points can a line and a circle share?
questions.explanation: Putting $$P + tA$$ into the circle's equation gives a quadratic in $$t$$, with $$0$$, $$1$$ or $$2$$ solutions as its discriminant is negative, zero or positive (:ref{#line-circle}).

questions.question: Where does the line $$(0, 1) + t(1, 1)$$ meet the circle $$x^2 + y^2 = 1$$?
When is a line tangent to a circle?
options: When it passes through the centre
When it meets the circle in exactly one point
When it meets the circle in two points
questions.explanation: That is the definition (:ref{#tangent-line}). The discriminant of the quadratic in $$t$$ is then $$0$$.

questions.question: A point $$P$$ is inside a circle. What is true of every line through $$P$$?
options: It meets the circle twice, once on each side of $$P$$
It is tangent to the circle
questions.explanation: The quadratic's constant term $$|P - C|^2 - r^2$$ is negative, so its two roots have opposite signs (:ref{#inside-point-line}): one meeting point on each side of $$P$$.

questions.question: What is $$(2, -3) \cdot (4, 1)$$?
questions.explanation: $$2 \cdot 4 + (-3) \cdot 1 = 5$$ (:ref{#dot-product}). A dot product is a number, not a point.

questions.question: Which direction is perpendicular to $$(2, 3)$$?
questions.explanation: $$(2, 3) \cdot (-3, 2) = -6 + 6 = 0$$ (:ref{#perpendicular-formula}). Swapping the numbers and changing one sign always works, and that's the quarter turn.

questions.question: A line has slope $$\frac{2}{3}$$. What slope does a perpendicular line have?
questions.explanation: Non-vertical lines are perpendicular exactly when their slopes multiply to $$-1$$ (:ref{#perpendicular-slopes}), and $$\frac{2}{3} \cdot \left(-\frac{3}{2}\right) = -1$$.

questions.question: Which formula holds for all points $$A$$ and $$B$$?
questions.explanation: Multiply out $$(A - B) \cdot (A - B)$$ (:ref{#difference-length}). The last option is the right-angle case, when $$A \cdot B = 0$$.

questions.question: How far is the point $$(1, 1)$$ from the line $$3x + 4y = 17$$?
questions.explanation: $$\frac{|3 + 4 - 17|}{\sqrt{9 + 16}} = \frac{10}{5} = 2$$ (:ref{#distance-to-line}). Forgetting to divide by $$\sqrt{a^2 + b^2} = 5$$ gives $$10$$.

questions.question: What is special about the closest point $$F$$ of a line to a point $$X$$?
options: $$F$$ is where the line meets the $$x$$-axis
$$F$$ is the midpoint of the line
The step $$X - F$$ is perpendicular to the line
questions.explanation: $$F$$ is the one point of the line with $$(X - F) \cdot A = 0$$ (:ref{#closest-point}), and then every other point is further away, by Pythagoras.

questions.question: How does the tangent to a circle at $$Q$$ meet the radius to $$Q$$?
questions.explanation: A line through a point of the circle is tangent exactly when it is perpendicular to the radius there (:ref{#tangent-perpendicular}).

questions.question: What does the guide on the rules for lines show?
options: That the rules taken from the picture hold for lines defined by formulas
That the picture rules are wrong
That lines are circles of infinite radius
That every line passes through the origin
questions.explanation: With lines, segments and rays defined by $$P + tA$$, every rule from the picture, such as two points fixing one line (:ref{#line-rule-two-points}), becomes a theorem.

questions.question: When is $$d(P, M) = d(P, Q) + d(Q, M)$$, for $$P \ne M$$?
options: Exactly when $$Q$$ lies on the line $$PM$$
Exactly when $$Q$$ lies on the segment $$PM$$
questions.explanation: A detour through $$Q$$ is no longer exactly when $$Q$$ is on the way (:ref{#triangle-equality}). A point of the line beyond $$M$$ makes the detour longer.

questions.question: When is $$as + bt = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2}\sqrt{s^2 + t^2}$$, for $$(a, b) \ne (0, 0)$$?
options: Exactly when $$(s, t) = c(a, b)$$ for some $$c$$
Exactly when $$(s, t) = c(a, b)$$ for some $$c \ge 0$$
questions.explanation: Equality needs $$(at - bs)^2 = 0$$ and $$as + bt \ge 0$$ (:ref{#product-bound-equality}). A negative multiple makes the left side negative.

questions.question: What does a zoom about any point do to a line?
options: Sends it onto a line parallel to it
Sends it onto a perpendicular line
Sends it to a single point
questions.explanation: $$Z_{r,Q}(P + tB) = Z_{r,Q}(P) + t(rB)$$, so the image is the line with direction $$rB$$, parallel to the first (:ref{#moves-keep-lines}). This proves the zoom rule about lines.

questions.question: Why is there exactly one line through a point $$X$$ perpendicular to the line $$P + tA$$?
options: Its direction must be a non-zero multiple of $$G_{90}(A) = (-a_2, a_1)$$
Because there is only one line through $$X$$
Because $$X$$ must be on the line
There are two, one each side
questions.explanation: Every direction $$B$$ with $$A \cdot B = 0$$ is a non-zero multiple of $$(-a_2, a_1)$$, and the line through $$X$$ with that direction is unique (:ref{#perpendicular-rules-proved}).

questions.question: What is the midpoint of $$(1, 0, 2)$$ and $$(3, 2, 0)$$, using $$P + \frac{1}{2}(Q - P)$$?
What are skew lines?
options: Lines that meet at an angle other than $$90^\circ$$
Lines in space that are not parallel and never meet
questions.explanation: That is the definition (:ref{#skew-lines}). In the plane, lines that aren't parallel always meet, so skew lines need space.

questions.question: Why do two lines in space usually fail to meet?
options: Lines in space are always parallel
Meeting needs three equations in only two unknowns $$t$$ and $$s$$
Lines in space have no direction
questions.explanation: $$P + tA = Q + sB$$ is one equation for each coordinate (:ref{#space-meeting}). Two unknowns can usually satisfy two equations, but not a third as well.

questions.question: In space, lines with directions $$(1, 2, -1)$$ and $$(3, -1, 1)$$ never meet. Are they perpendicular?
options: No: the directions are perpendicular, but perpendicular lines must meet
Yes, since the dot product is $$0$$
No, since the dot product isn't $$0$$
questions.explanation: $$3 - 2 - 1 = 0$$, so the directions are perpendicular (:ref{#space-dot}). Lines in space are perpendicular when they meet and their directions are (:ref{#space-perpendicular}), so these skew lines are not.
